questions.prompt: No animal was domesticated earlier than the dog.
questions.evidence: Dogs were the first animals to be domesticated
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says dogs were the first animals to be domesticated, which means no other animal was domesticated before them.

questions.prompt: Early farmers brought wild cats onto their land to deal with mice.
questions.evidence: which moved in of their own accord and appear to have largely domesticated themselves
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says the wild cats came by themselves because of the mice. People did not bring them in, so the statement contradicts the passage.

questions.prompt: When dogs and owners look at each other, oxytocin rises in the owners but not in the dogs.
questions.evidence: rise in both the human and the dog
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says oxytocin levels go up in both the person and the dog, not only in the person.

questions.prompt: All of the volunteers in Kearney's study already owned cats.
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says Kearney used forty volunteers and some of them stroked a cat. It never says whether any of them owned cats themselves.

questions.prompt: Mehta carried out his interviews in more than one location.
questions.evidence: interviewing dog walkers in three city parks
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says Mehta interviewed dog walkers in three different parks, so his research took place in more than one place.

questions.prompt: Abernathy's greyhound had a successful career as a racing dog.
questions.explanation: Paragraph E says the greyhound used to be a racing dog. It says nothing about whether it won races or did well, so we cannot know.

questions.prompt: Some people give up newly adopted pets because they had not realised how much effort the animals would need.
questions.evidence: some pets are handed back within months because their new owners underestimated the commitment involved
questions.explanation: Paragraph G says charities find that some pets are returned because the owners did not expect how much commitment was needed. 'Underestimated the commitment' means the same as not realising how much effort was needed.

questions.prompt: Which TWO of the following does the writer give as reasons why early dogs were valued?

options.text: assisting people when they hunted
alerting groups to coming threats
pulling ploughs on early farms
protecting stores of grain
catching mice near human homes

questions.evidence: helping with hunting and by warning of approaching danger
questions.explanation: Paragraph B says early dogs helped with hunting and warned of danger. Pulling ploughs and guarding grain appear in Paragraph A as jobs modern pets do not do, and catching mice is linked to cats, not dogs.

questions.prompt: Which TWO results does Kearney report for the volunteers who stroked a cat?

options.text: They described themselves as more relaxed.
Their heart rates settled down sooner.
Their oxytocin levels went up sharply.
They did better on the arithmetic task.
They asked to spend longer with the cat.

questions.evidence: reported feeling calmer afterwards, and their heart rates returned to normal more quickly
questions.explanation: Paragraph C says these volunteers felt calmer and their heart rates returned to normal faster. Oxytocin is mentioned only in other research about dogs, and the arithmetic task was done before the cat, not measured afterwards.

questions.prompt: Which TWO points does the writer make about giving pets to children?

options.text: The evidence for benefits is less clear than many parents think.
Adults often end up doing the daily care after interest fades.
Rabbits are the most suitable first pet for young children.
Children with pets tend to take more exercise than others.
Looking after an animal always makes children more responsible.

questions.evidence: although the research is more mixed than many parents assume. In practice, the daily work of feeding a rabbit and cleaning out its hutch frequently falls to adults once the novelty has worn off
questions.explanation: Paragraph F says the research is more mixed than parents expect and that adults often take over the care once the novelty is gone. The rabbit is only an example, not a recommendation, and extra exercise is linked to dog owners in Paragraph D, not to children.

questions.prompt: Mehta says a dog functions as a ______, making it easier for its owner to chat with people they do not know.
questions.evidence: a dog works as what he calls a 'social passport'
questions.explanation: Paragraph D says Mehta calls a dog a 'social passport' because strangers stop to talk to dog walkers.

questions.prompt: After losing his wife, Abernathy had stopped paying attention to ______ and most other things.
questions.evidence: I had stopped bothering with mealtimes, stopped bothering with most things
questions.explanation: In Paragraph E, Abernathy says he had stopped bothering with mealtimes; 'stopped paying attention to' restates 'stopped bothering with'.

questions.prompt: Besides being expensive and making holidays harder, pets can cause ______ in some people.
questions.evidence: Animals cost money, restrict holidays and can trigger allergies.
questions.explanation: Paragraph G lists the costs of pets: money, limits on holidays and allergies. 'Cause' restates 'trigger'.

questions.prompt: In the writer's view, what pets give above all is an uncommon form of ______.
questions.evidence: What pets offer, more than anything, is a kind of acceptance that is rare elsewhere in life
questions.explanation: Paragraph H says the main thing pets offer is acceptance that is rare elsewhere. 'Above all' restates 'more than anything' and 'uncommon' restates 'rare'.

people.name: Siobhan Kearney
people.role: psychologist who studied the effect of stroking a cat on stressed volunteers

people.name: Arjun Mehta
people.role: sociologist who interviewed dog walkers in city parks

people.name: Rhys Abernathy
people.role: retired engineer who adopted a former racing greyhound after his wife died

paragraphs.text: Walk down almost any residential street and you will pass evidence of a quiet devotion: a bag of dog biscuits in a shopping basket, a scratching post glimpsed through a window, a hutch at the bottom of a garden. In many wealthy countries, roughly half of all households now include at least one animal, and owners happily spend sums on food, toys and veterinary care that would have astonished their grandparents. Yet from a purely practical point of view, most modern pets do very little. They do not pull ploughs, guard grain or bring home dinner. So why do so many of us choose to share our homes with them?
paragraphs.label: A

paragraphs.text: Part of the answer lies in history. Dogs were the first animals to be domesticated, descending from wolves that began living alongside human groups at least 15,000 years ago. Those early dogs earned their place by helping with hunting and by warning of approaching danger. Cats arrived by a different route. When people began farming and storing grain, the stores attracted mice, and the mice attracted wild cats, which moved in of their own accord and appear to have largely domesticated themselves. For thousands of years, then, the relationship was essentially a working arrangement. Keeping animals mainly for company, rather than for the jobs they could do, became widespread only much later, largely within the last two centuries.
paragraphs.label: B

paragraphs.text: That shift makes more sense once you look at what happens inside us when we spend time with an animal. Researchers have found that when dogs and their owners gaze at each other, levels of oxytocin, a hormone linked to the bond between parents and babies, rise in both the human and the dog. In a smaller study of her own, the psychologist Dr Siobhan Kearney asked forty volunteers to complete a stressful arithmetic task and then spend ten minutes either sitting quietly or stroking a friendly cat. Those who had been with the cat reported feeling calmer afterwards, and their heart rates returned to normal more quickly. Kearney is careful not to overstate the result. 'It was one group of people in one laboratory,' she says. 'But it fits what owners have been telling us for years.'
paragraphs.label: C

paragraphs.text: Pets also reshape our days in ways we hardly notice. A dog needs walking whether or not its owner feels like going out, and studies have repeatedly found that dog owners are, on average, more physically active than people without dogs. Just as important, perhaps, is who they meet along the way. The sociologist Arjun Mehta spent a year interviewing dog walkers in three city parks and concluded that a dog works as what he calls a 'social passport'. Strangers who would never speak to a lone adult will happily stop to ask a dog's name or age, and many of Mehta's interviewees said they knew far more of their neighbours since getting a dog. Cat owners, he admits, were not part of the research.
paragraphs.label: D

paragraphs.text: For people living alone, these effects can matter a great deal. Rhys Abernathy, a retired engineer, adopted a former racing greyhound eighteen months after his wife died. 'I had stopped bothering with mealtimes, stopped bothering with most things,' he recalls. 'Suddenly there was someone who needed feeding at seven every morning.' He insists that the dog did not replace human company; instead, it got him out of the house, where human company could find him again.
paragraphs.label: E

paragraphs.text: Children are often given a pet in the hope that it will teach them responsibility and kindness. There is some evidence that looking after an animal helps young people understand that others have needs and feelings, although the research is more mixed than many parents assume. In practice, the daily work of feeding a rabbit and cleaning out its hutch frequently falls to adults once the novelty has worn off. That is worth remembering before anyone promises that a new pet will be entirely the child's responsibility.
paragraphs.label: F

paragraphs.text: None of this means that a pet is a cure for every difficulty, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Animals cost money, restrict holidays and can trigger allergies. Their lives are also far shorter than ours, so owners must expect, sooner or later, to grieve. Animal welfare charities report that some pets are handed back within months because their new owners underestimated the commitment involved. A pet chosen on impulse, to fill a gap that really calls for something else, may end up making both animal and owner unhappy.
paragraphs.label: G

paragraphs.text: Still, the appeal endures, and perhaps the simplest explanation is the best one. With other people we are always being judged, at least a little, on our looks, our success or our conversation. A dog waiting at the door or a cat settling on a lap asks for none of that. What pets offer, more than anything, is a kind of acceptance that is rare elsewhere in life, and for many owners that alone is worth every vet's bill.
paragraphs.label: H

section.text:
What Our Animals Give Us

A. Walk down almost any residential street and you will pass evidence of a quiet devotion: a bag of dog biscuits in a shopping basket, a scratching post glimpsed through a window, a hutch at the bottom of a garden. In many wealthy countries, roughly half of all households now include at least one animal, and owners happily spend sums on food, toys and veterinary care that would have astonished their grandparents. Yet from a purely practical point of view, most modern pets do very little. They do not pull ploughs, guard grain or bring home dinner. So why do so many of us choose to share our homes with them?

B. Part of the answer lies in history. Dogs were the first animals to be domesticated, descending from wolves that began living alongside human groups at least 15,000 years ago. Those early dogs earned their place by helping with hunting and by warning of approaching danger. Cats arrived by a different route. When people began farming and storing grain, the stores attracted mice, and the mice attracted wild cats, which moved in of their own accord and appear to have largely domesticated themselves. For thousands of years, then, the relationship was essentially a working arrangement. Keeping animals mainly for company, rather than for the jobs they could do, became widespread only much later, largely within the last two centuries.

C. That shift makes more sense once you look at what happens inside us when we spend time with an animal. Researchers have found that when dogs and their owners gaze at each other, levels of oxytocin, a hormone linked to the bond between parents and babies, rise in both the human and the dog. In a smaller study of her own, the psychologist Dr Siobhan Kearney asked forty volunteers to complete a stressful arithmetic task and then spend ten minutes either sitting quietly or stroking a friendly cat. Those who had been with the cat reported feeling calmer afterwards, and their heart rates returned to normal more quickly. Kearney is careful not to overstate the result. 'It was one group of people in one laboratory,' she says. 'But it fits what owners have been telling us for years.'

D. Pets also reshape our days in ways we hardly notice. A dog needs walking whether or not its owner feels like going out, and studies have repeatedly found that dog owners are, on average, more physically active than people without dogs. Just as important, perhaps, is who they meet along the way. The sociologist Arjun Mehta spent a year interviewing dog walkers in three city parks and concluded that a dog works as what he calls a 'social passport'. Strangers who would never speak to a lone adult will happily stop to ask a dog's name or age, and many of Mehta's interviewees said they knew far more of their neighbours since getting a dog. Cat owners, he admits, were not part of the research.

E. For people living alone, these effects can matter a great deal. Rhys Abernathy, a retired engineer, adopted a former racing greyhound eighteen months after his wife died. 'I had stopped bothering with mealtimes, stopped bothering with most things,' he recalls. 'Suddenly there was someone who needed feeding at seven every morning.' He insists that the dog did not replace human company; instead, it got him out of the house, where human company could find him again.

F. Children are often given a pet in the hope that it will teach them responsibility and kindness. There is some evidence that looking after an animal helps young people understand that others have needs and feelings, although the research is more mixed than many parents assume. In practice, the daily work of feeding a rabbit and cleaning out its hutch frequently falls to adults once the novelty has worn off. That is worth remembering before anyone promises that a new pet will be entirely the child's responsibility.

G. None of this means that a pet is a cure for every difficulty, and it would be dishonest to pretend otherwise. Animals cost money, restrict holidays and can trigger allergies. Their lives are also far shorter than ours, so owners must expect, sooner or later, to grieve. Animal welfare charities report that some pets are handed back within months because their new owners underestimated the commitment involved. A pet chosen on impulse, to fill a gap that really calls for something else, may end up making both animal and owner unhappy.

H. Still, the appeal endures, and perhaps the simplest explanation is the best one. With other people we are always being judged, at least a little, on our looks, our success or our conversation. A dog waiting at the door or a cat settling on a lap asks for none of that. What pets offer, more than anything, is a kind of acceptance that is rare elsewhere in life, and for many owners that alone is worth every vet's bill.
